title: Comments of the Illinois Commerce Commission in support of the Complaint of Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. under EL26-98.

documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                  BEFORE THE
                    FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


Pennsylvania Public Utility                    )
Commission                                     )
                                               )
v.                                             )                    Docket No. EL26-98-000
                                               )
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                    )


              COMMENTS OF THE ILLINOIS COMMERCE COMMISSION

       Pursuant to the notice of filing issued August 18, 2026, and the notice of extension of

comment date issued September 1, 2026, the Illinois Commerce Commission (ICC) hereby

submits these comments in support of the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission’s (PAPUC)

complaint against PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (PJM) filed on August 17, 2026, in the above-

captioned docket (PAPUC Complaint). The ICC filed a notice of intervention on August 19,

2026, and, therefore, is a party to this proceeding.

       The PAPUC Complaint highlights existing flaws in how PJM determines benefit-cost

(BC) ratios for Market Efficiency Projects (MEP) to the detriment of consumers, not just in

Pennsylvania, but also in Illinois and throughout the region. In their complaint, the PAPUC

underscores that PJM’s approach does not conform to industry standards. PJM’s approach has

selected projects that raise costs in aggregate across the footprint. The PAPUC offers

straightforward solutions that PJM should implement.

       The ICC is a strong supporter of both competition and transmission development for the

purpose of advancing consumer interests, efficiencies, and reliability on the grid. These

comments support the PAPUC’s proposed changes for improving PJM’s process to enable
 efficient transmission projects to be properly selected while protecting ratepayers in Illinois and

across the region and ensuring the markets work effectively.

          Specifically, the Commission should direct PJM to include the impact in all (benefitting

and non-benefitting) zones when calculating consumer benefits for the purposes of market

efficiency projects by either (1) deleting from PJM’s Schedule 6, Section 1.5.7 of the Operating

Agreement, the red-lined language from the definitions of “Change in Load Energy Payment”

and “Change in Load Capacity Payment” as set forth in the PAPUC Complaint at pages 2-3, or

(2) alternatively, order PJM to revise its Operating Agreement to add the increase in Load Energy

Payment and Load Capacity Payment to the denominator of the Benefit-Cost Ratio, in the

definition of Total Enhancement Cost, as set forth in the PAPUC Complaint at page 3. As

discussed below, the current calculation violates ratemaking mandates of the Federal Power Act

(FPA), distorts generation resource development, and challenges holistic planning for prudent

transmission investment.

          I.      Comments

                  A. PJM’s Consumer Benefits Calculation for its Market Efficiency Projects
                     is Flawed, Unjust and Unreasonable, and Unduly Discriminatory and
                     Preferential in Violation of the Federal Power Act.

          The PAPUC Complaint demonstrates that PJM’s Schedule 6, Section 1.5.7 of PJM’s

Operating Agreement is unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory or preferential in the

manner it selects MEPs. 1 The ICC agrees. PJM’s consumer benefit calculation contains a

flawed BC ratio calculation that only takes into account the zones that benefit from the project,

disregarding those that may be harmed by the project increasing their costs. By considering only



1
    PAPUC Complaint at 1.

                                                  2
 the potential beneficiaries of a project without considering harm to others in project selection,

PJM’s process is unjust and unreasonable, unduly discriminatory and preferential in violation of

the FPA. 2

         In relevant part, Section 205 of the FPA requires that:

                  All rates and charges made, demanded, or received by any public utility for
                  or in connection with the transmission or sale of electric energy subject to
                  the jurisdiction of the Commission, and all rules and regulations affecting
                  or pertaining to such rates or charges shall be just and reasonable, and any
                  such rate or charge that is not just and reasonable is hereby declared to be
                  unlawful. 3
and
                  No public utility shall, with respect to any transmission or sale subject to
                  the jurisdiction of the Commission, (1) make or grant any undue preference
                  or advantage to any person or subject any person to any undue prejudice or
                  disadvantage, or (2) maintain any unreasonable difference in rates, charges,
                  service, facilities, or in any other respect, either as between localities or as
                  between classes of service. 4
Further, Section 206 of the FPA states:
                  Whenever the Commission, after a hearing had upon its own motion or upon
                  complaint, shall find that any rate, charge, or classification, demanded,
                  observed, charged, or collected by any public utility for any transmission or
                  sale subject to the jurisdiction of the Commission, or that any rule,
                  regulation, practice, or contract affecting such rate, charge, or classification
                  is unjust, unreasonable, unduly discriminatory or preferential, the
                  Commission shall determine the just and reasonable rate, charge,
                  classification, rule, regulation, practice, or contract to be thereafter observed
                  and in force, and shall fix the same by order. 5

         PJM’s current practice and related tariff language for selection criteria of MEP projects is

clearly a rule and practice affecting the transmission rates that is unjust, unreasonable, unduly

discriminatory and preferential in violation of the FPA. Selecting transmission projects that only

  16 U.S.C. § 824d(a), (b).
3
  16 U.S.C. § 824d(a).
4
  16 U.S.C. § 824d(b).
5

                                                     3
 benefit certain zones while ignoring the harm to other zones through higher Locational Marginal

Prices (LMPs) violates these requirements and is unlawful. As PAPUC witness Zachary Ming

(Witness Ming) testified, “it discriminates between consumers in the PJM region.” 6

        In particular, PJM’s MEP selection process with its skewed BC calculations discriminates

against consumers in Illinois. Witness Ming found one recent candidate MEP project, for

example, that benefits every zone except the ComEd zone in PJM’s recent Regional

Transmission Expansion Planning (RTEP) process. While other PJM customers would receive a

total benefit of $170 million, ComEd customers, on the other hand, would incur a cost increase

of around $150 million as a result of the project’s construction. 7 The aggregate load payment

benefits to all zones total, therefore, only $20 million, not the $169.8 million asserted by PJM,

with a BC ratio of only “0.24, not 1.99.” 89 As Witness Ming and the PJM Independent Market

Monitor separately concluded, the “project should have been rejected.” 10 This ComEd example

underscores that the MEP BC process is unjust and unreasonable, and it illustrates the significant

negative impacts of PJM’s flawed MEP process.

        Customers in the ComEd zone should not have to bear a disproportionate portion of the

costs of PJM transmission projects. 11 The process unlawfully shifts costs from the cost causers

to others who are harmed. That is improper. As set forth in the PJM cost allocation case Illinois

Commerce Commission et al. v FERC, the Seventh Circuit said, “FERC is not authorized to




6
   PAPUC Complaint, Attachment A, Direct Testimony of Zachary Ming (Ming Testimony), at 3.
7
   Ming Testimony at 31-32 (Witness Ming analyzing Goalders Creek substation expansion, Museville-Smith
Mountain upgrade, and the Multi-Driver project in the COMED-NIPSCO-AEP area, RTEP proposals 525, 733, and
644+908, PJM 2023 RTEP).
8
  Ming Testimony at 33, note 39 (citing Monitoring Analytics, 2024 State of the Market Report for PJM, at 715).
9
   Id. at 33.
10
   Id.
11
   See Monitoring Analytics. LLC, 2026 Quarterly State of the Market Report for PJM: January through March, at
826.

                                                       4
 approve a pricing scheme that requires a group of utilities to pay for facilities from which its

members derive no benefits, or benefits that are trivial in relation to the costs sought to be shifted

to its members. ‘[A]ll approved rates [must] reflect to some degree the costs actually caused by

the customer who must pay them.’” 12 While this court decision addressed cost allocation, this

fairness consideration is valid in transmission project selection as well.

        In fact, the United States Court of Appeals has already indicated the importance of

examining both the upstream and downstream impacts of transmission projects that mitigate

congestion. In Citadel FNGE Ltd. v. FERC, the Commission reviewed congestion pricing and

found, among other things, that increasing prices to one set of customers while the value

benefits flow to a different customer is unjust and unreasonable. 13 In that case, the Commission

determined that one important component of the wholesale rate—the congestion cost—was

unjust and unreasonable as applied. 14 On petition for review, the court explained, “. . . the

Commission concluded that increased prices on one side of the balance without any value on the

other side of the scale—all pain and no gain—were unjust and unreasonable.” 15 The court

agreed. 16 In denying the petitions for review, the court said that PJM’s penalty factor could not

work as designed because it increased costs to consumers without a commensurate benefit, so the

968 F.2d 1295, 1300 (D.C.Cir.1992)); Transmission Access Policy Study Group v. FERC, 225 F.3d 667, 708 (D.C.
Cir. 2000); Pacific Gas & Elec. Co. v. FERC, 373 F.3d 1315, 1320–21 (D.C. Cir. 2004).
13
   Citadel FNGE Ltd. v. FERC, 77 F.4th 842, 855 (D.C. Cir. 2023) (Citadel).
14
   Id; See also San Diego Gas & Elec. Co. v. FERC, 913 F.3d 127, 138 (D.C. Cir. 2019) (upholding Commission's

NextEra Energy Res., LLC v. FERC, 898 F.3d 14, 21 (D.C. Cir. 2018) ("We defer to the Commission's determination
that the renewable exemption effectuates the market's primary purpose by sending the correct demand signals to new
entrants and by protecting consumers from excessive rates.").
15
   Citadel at 855 (“[t]hat was ‘a principled and reasoned decision supported by the evidentiary record[.]’)(citing
MISO Transmission Owners v. FERC, 45 F.4th 248, 258 (D.C. Cir. 2022) (quoting Emera Maine v. FERC, 854 F.3d
9, 22 (D.C. Cir. 2022)).
16
   Citadel at 855-56 (“Penalty Factor was unjust and unreasonable not just because of how much it increased the
wholesale rate, but because it caused that increase for no justifiable purpose.”).

                                                        5
 Commission “reasonably found that its application . . . was unjust and unreasonable.” 17 The

court further explained that “the Commission found that the application of the Penalty Factor

was unjust and unreasonable not just because of how much it increased the wholesale rate, but

because it caused that increase for no justifiable purpose. That comfortably fits the definition of

unjust and unreasonable.” 18

        Similarly in PJM’s MEP process, PJM recognizes only one side of the congestion

equation and ignores the other, the result of which is that one set of customers do not receive any

benefits yet have increased costs. This results in an unlawful increase in cost to those ratepayers

for no justifiable purpose. 19 PJM projects should not require one zone that is burdened with

increased costs and no benefits to subsidize a zone benefiting from the project, like the example

of the MEP project impacts on ComEd customers. Forcing ComEd zone ratepayers to pay any

amount of a project that has been shown to cause them harm is neither just nor reasonable and is

unduly discriminatory. PJM’s current approach, therefore, is unjust and unreasonable and must

be corrected.

        While PJM must make changes to ensure that MEPs are selected in a fair manner, the

MEPs can be a useful tool when properly implemented. As noted in Witness Ming’s testimony,

“market efficiency projects are designed to improve the system economics by facilitating the

dispatch of lowest cost generation.” 20 Dispatching the lowest cost resources through

transmission lines to benefit ratepayers is reasonable, and mitigating congestion is a necessary

goal. 21 As Witness Ming demonstrates, however, PJM’s selection process allows transmission


17
   Id. at 847.
18
   Citadel at 856.
19
   Id.
20
   Ming Testimony at 6.
21
   PJM Operating Agreement, Schedule 6, Section 1.5.7 (b).

                                                       6
 projects to be selected that cause significant financial harm to the region overall while benefitting

only a subset of the region. While transmission development is an important tool to develop

competitive markets for the region, ensuring the benefits calculation reflects the regional impacts

to the entire system, not just the benefits to specific nodes that see lower prices by the resolution

of the congestion constraint, is imperative. For too long now, PJM has obscured the costs of

MEP projects, looking only at one side of the equation – often to the detriment of consumers in

Illinois. This must be corrected.

           The ICC agrees with the PAPUC that PJM’s BC calculations for selecting MEPs are

flawed. As noted in the PAPUC Complaint, PJM calculates MEPs’ benefits by considering both

the change in load energy and load capacity payments that would result from those projects being

constructed, but it only looks at the benefits not the harm. 22 The implicit assumption is that all

MEPs will lower prices just by relieving congesting and allowing more energy to flow, but MEPs

do not always decrease prices in all zones. There are instances where selected transmission

projects move energy from locations that are upstream from congestion to other load, where that

shift in power along transmission lines can actually raise prices in these upstream locations. This

potential pricing outcome, however, is not incorporated into the PJM’s MEP BC calculation

process – a deviation from many other RTOs’ process for selecting market efficiency projects.

Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO), New York-ISO (NYISO), Southwest Power

Pool (SPP), California-ISO (CAISO), and ISO-New England (ISO-NE) all look at holistic cost

impacts for their comparable MEPs. 23 Hence, PJM’s calculations do not consider the varied

footprint-wide impacts MEPs could have on RTO LMPs. By failing to include price increases



22
     PAPUC Complaint at 13, 14.
23
     PAPUC Complaint at 24-29.

                                                  7
 for zones that are upstream for price congestion, PJM is overstating the MEPs benefits for the

region as a whole. PJM’s selections ignore that some zones will pay disproportionate costs for

projects that benefit other zones.

        One way that PJM attempted previously to justify the calculation of its BC in this way

was its assertion that this methodology better aligns cost allocation to zones that are directly

benefiting. 24 However, the PAPUC correctly argues the methodology is not about cost allocation

but about project selection. 25 The PJM MEP BC calculation methodology is failing to fully

incorporate all the potential costs of a given project, and therefore the BC ratio derived by that

method is inaccurate and misleading. In effect, PJM is selecting MEPs that sometimes are

harming zones upstream of congestion to a degree that would move the project’s BC ratio below

1.25, the level required for selection. In other words, some MEPs selected by PJM cause such

significant upstream impact on LMPs that it more than offsets the benefits of any alleviated

downstream congestion. 26 PJM is, in at least some cases, building transmission that lowers

LMPs for some zones while then raising costs substantially for other zones. By doing so, PJM is

not so much building too much transmission as it building the wrong transmission - and

unjustifiably picking winners and losers.

        Of note, and emphasizing the flawed approach PJM has taken, PJM’s MEP BC

calculation is an industry outlier. No other RTO’s project selection process excludes zones that

are financially harmed while including only zones that will benefit with lower prices from

transmission construction of an MEP (or comparable project type). 27 Notably, MISO, which


24
   Id. at 31.
25
   Id. at 15.
26
   Id. at 9.
27
   Ming Testimony at 13 (“No other ISO in North America calculates consumer benefits for only a subset of
consumers.”), Appendix (survey of other regions’ approaches).

                                                        8
 includes Illinois utilities and ratepayers, considers footprint-wide price impacts in its

transmission selection calculation. 28 MISO plans for proactive, long-term transmission building,

and the ICC has supported MISO’s recent transmission efforts. PJM should learn from MISO’s

approach and incorporate increases in zonal costs into the MEP selection process.

        Contrastingly, PJM’s faulty approach to the MEP BC calculation contradicts PJM’s

mission to reduce congestion and costs across its footprint. 29 The ICC agrees that PJM should

work to contain congestion region-wide, but congestion control does not mean addressing every

instance of congestion across the footprint – particularly where doing so results in economic

inefficiencies without adequate justification. PJM must develop a reasonable BC calculation that

is in line with PJM’s mission vis-à-vis congestion management while fully accounting for

impacts on all consumers – those at both ends of the line. Considering the upstream cost impacts

of MEP lines would be fully in line with PJM’s cost containment mission of achieving an

economically efficient system. The Commission should direct PJM to do so.

                 B. PJM’s Flawed MEP Selection Process is Sending Distorted Price Signals
                 that may Discourage Resource Development.

        PJM’s flawed MEP selection process causes at least two significant problems: (1)

increased overall (and local) costs as discussed above and (2) muted price signals that may

reduce incentives to build needed resources. 30 PJM’s methodology could be suppressing price

signals to build new generation and utilize other resources by inappropriately building

transmission when generation build out or other options may be a better alternative. 31 If

transmission build out lowers the cost of LMPs in one area even though if evaluated correctly it


28
   MISO Tariff, Attachment FF-7.I.A, pp. 513-16.
29
   PJM Operating Agreement, Schedule 6, Section 1.5.7 (b).
30
   PAPUC Complaint at 10.
31
   Id.

                                                       9
 would have been cheaper to build generation, then the transmission built and the resulting

congestion reduction is suppressing price signals that would aid the market in determining where

generation or other resources need to be added. The need to build generation and increase other

resources’ output has been magnified by increased forecasts of load growth, especially related to

data center load growth. 32

        Generation construction is complicated and hinges on many elements including price

signals, siting, permitting, supply chain issues, financing, and the interconnection queue. LMPs

are not the only factor for new generation to be built; pricing to recoup investments is also a

significant factor. The Commission must balance these necessary price signals for transmission

and generation with issues of affordability and rate impacts on consumers. Getting the selection

process right can help us achieve economically efficient outcomes. The PAPUC complaint notes

that “the current market efficiency selection construct serves to dampen the market signals to

build generation close to the load it serves” 33 As discussed above, by not including the higher

energy costs to zones upstream from the congestion in the selection process, PJM’s MEP

calculations overstate the benefits of some transmission projects. These transmission projects

then bring lower cost energy that lower LMPs in zones downstream from congestion, thereby

discouraging new generation or other resource development where it is needed. 34 This approach

may exacerbate resource adequacy shortfalls, reliability risks, and exorbitant prices resulting in

rates that are unjust and unreasonable.

             This price distortion is bad for the markets. As a retail choice state, Illinois relies heavily

on wholesale energy and capacity markets. Disrupting LMP signals generates concern that the

needed information to build the appropriate resources in the appropriate locations is being

distorted. LMPs are an important data point to signal where resources are needed. Suppressing

price signals discourages resource development where it is needed, creates further uncertainty in

the markets, and may exacerbate PJM’s reliability risks.

                   C. The ICC Encourages Holistic Transmission Planning and Prudent
                   Transmission Investment, but PJM Should Make the Corrections to Ensure
                   Just and Reasonable Rates.

            The PAPUC Complaint explains that the purpose of the MEP is to “satisfy the

Commission-endorsed goal to reduce costs for customers and allow generation to be built at the

lowest cost location for the benefit of customers.” 35 The ICC agrees that the “appropriate

measurement criteria to accomplish that goal is all-in cost for all customers.” 36 The ICC

supports competition as a tool to discipline prices. The ICC has supported energy markets and

competitive transmission building for years. The ICC reiterates its support for MEPs as a useful

tool to facilitate productive competition among generators and benefit consumers – to the extent

that the BC calculation is fair and the selection process is properly conducted.

            While PJM’s current MEP BC calculation approach is flawed, the ICC agrees with the

PAPUC that simple corrections can be made to fix the problems. The ICC remains supportive of

the MEP process more broadly. Transmission planning remains an important aspect of reliability

and cost control in PJM. The ICC continues to support regional and holistic transmission

planning, including PJM’s Regional Transmission Plan (RTEP) and more recent Order 1920 long



35
     Id. at 20.
36
     Id.

                                                      11
 term transmission planning efforts. 37 The ICC strongly believes that transmission is a valuable

tool for reliability and cost control.

        While the ICC supports needed transmission development, the ICC also believes that

proper transmission planning that includes fair project selection is critical to efficiency.

Transmission investment must be prudent and in the interest of ratepayers. PJM should build the

most efficient transmission in the given footprint conditions. PJM has a range of tools with

which to meet its transmission needs, including baseline reliability projects, market efficiency

projects, and supplemental projects. Each of these projects serves an important need and

function, and the ICC supports PJM prudently pursuing these various project types to ensure a

robust transmission grid. It is important, however, that PJM look for the most economic

solutions. The first step in this case is to correct its flawed BC calculations to ensure a fair

process and just and reasonable rates for all consumers. PJM’s MEP BC calculations must take

into account the broader costs that come with these projects and fairly account for those in a

transparent manner to ensure that transmission investment is prudent, economic and efficient.

        The ICC, therefore, urges the Commission to order PJM to take the corrective measures

the PAPUC requested in its complaint. The Commission should direct PJM to include the impact

in all (benefitting and non-benefitting) zones when calculating consumer benefits for the

purposes of market efficiency projects by either (1) deleting from PJM’s Schedule 6, Section

1.5.7 of the Operating Agreement, the red-lined language from the definitions of “Change in

Load Energy Payment” and “Change in Load Capacity Payment” as set forth in the PAPUC

61,028 (2022).

                                                     12
 Complaint at pages 2-3, or (2) alternatively, order PJM to revise its Operating Agreement to add

the increase in Load Energy Payment and Load Capacity Payment to the denominator of the

Benefit-Cost Ratio, in the definition of Total Enhancement Cost, as set forth in the PAPUC

Complaint at page 3.

        II.    Conclusion
       WHEREFORE, for all the reasons explained above, the ICC respectfully requests that the

Commission consider these comments in support of the PAPUC Complaint. The ICC further

requests any and all other appropriate relief.
